answer:
**Speech recognition must align a long audio sequence with a shorter token sequence.** A spoken word spans many frames, and the exact frame-to-label alignment is usually not provided. CTC, RNN-T, and attention encoder–decoders solve this alignment/generation problem differently. [1](https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~graves/icml_2006.pdf)

CTC predicts frame-level labels plus blanks and sums over compatible alignments. Repeated labels/blanks collapse into the output string. Frame predictions can be computed in parallel under its conditional structure, though beam search with language-model integration can still involve sequential decoding work.

RNN-T combines an acoustic encoder with a prediction network conditioned on previous output labels and a joint network, supporting a different alignment model often useful for streaming. An attention encoder–decoder reads encoded audio while generating text autoregressively; Whisper is a prominent example of that broad family. [2](https://arxiv.org/abs/1211.3711) [3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.04356)

**Why silence can produce words.** An autoregressive decoder has strong language-pattern knowledge. When acoustic evidence is weak, it may continue plausible text or repeat patterns rather than reliably output nothing. This is a possible failure mode, not a statement that every silent input always causes a loop.

Evaluate silence, background noise, accents, partial utterances, and streaming latency. Add appropriate no-speech detection, decoding controls, and confidence/abstention behavior. Word error rate on clean complete recordings does not capture hallucinated text during silence or the user experience of delayed streaming transcription.

**Technical details and references.**

CTC predicts frame-level label/blank distributions and sums over alignments that collapse to the same transcript. Its conditional-independence assumption permits parallel frame scoring; decoding with a language model or beam can still be sequential. RNN-T adds a label-history prediction network and marginalizes time/label alignments, making it suitable for streaming. Whisper uses an autoregressive attention-based decoder over audio features. [1](https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~graves/icml_2006.pdf) [2](https://arxiv.org/abs/1211.3711) [3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.04356)

$$p_{CTC}(y\mid x)=\sum_{\pi:\mathcal B(\pi)=y}\prod_t p(\pi_t\mid x).$$

On silence or weak audio, an autoregressive language prior can dominate and generate plausible unsupported text. Voice activity detection, no-speech thresholds, repetition checks, and appropriate decoding mitigate this; they do not prove every transcript is grounded. Compare latency, alignment assumptions, robustness, and language-model integration.
